content: 1. The transition from vertical programs addressing diarrheal diseases to the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) has broadened the scope of interventions. IMCI includes essential messages on basic nutrition, micronutrient supplementation programs, routine immunizations under the Expanded Programme on Immunization, and case management for acute respiratory infections, diarrheal diseases, and malaria. 2. Community-level water and sanitation interventions, along with investments in technology, community engagement, and behavioral change, remain underfunded and are closely linked to poverty. 3. Comparative analysis of three community-led or community-directed initiatives highlights their similarities and differences, which can be used to develop implementation research models that directly benefit communities affected by zoonotic infections. 4. The One Health concept emphasizes the integration of human and animal health resources. This approach facilitates better surveillance, diagnosis, and control of zoonoses by considering human and animal health together. It also improves access to health resources for impoverished populations and addresses the needs of their livestock. 5. Cost-sharing proportional to the benefits gained by each sector could enhance the implementation of the One Health approach. Generating data on the societal and economic impacts of zoonotic diseases, such as stigma and fear, is essential. Examples include cysticercosis, echinococcosis, brucellosis, and rabies. 6. Zoonotic diseases contribute to the burden of non-communicable diseases, including neurological disorders, liver disease, cancer, and injuries. Case studies include cysticercosis (epilepsy, headaches), echinococcosis and schistosomiasis (liver disease), foodborne trematodes (biliary and hepatic cancer), toxoplasmosis (schizophrenia, congenital abnormalities), and rabies (injuries). 7. Mass chemotherapy plays a critical role in treating parasitic and bacterial diseases, both individually and through mass drug administration (MDA). While praziquantel is effective against trematode and cestode infections, there is a need for improved drugs, combinations, and regimens to enhance efficacy and reduce transmission risks. 8. Preventive chemotherapy strategies for non-zoonotic neglected diseases have been developed by WHO, but these approaches have not been widely applied to zoonotic helminth infections. However, mass praziquantel distribution has been successful in controlling Schistosoma japonicum in China and the Philippines and eliminating S. mekongi in Cambodia. 9. Triclabendazole, donated by Novartis, is used for mass drug administration in endemic areas of fascioliasis in Bolivia and Peru. Its single-dose regimen (10 mg/kg) makes it suitable for MDA. 10. For cystic echinococcosis in humans, long-term high-dose treatment with albendazole (10 mg/kg/day) or mebendazole (40 mg/kg/day) damages cysts but is parasitostatic rather than parasiticidal. Albendazole is more effective due to better absorption. Approximately one-third of patients are cured, and many experience cyst size reduction. 11. Mass treatment of dogs with praziquantel (5 mg/kg) remains the treatment of choice for adult tapeworm infections, as demonstrated in successful control campaigns in Cyprus, Iceland, and New Zealand. Deworming dogs, combined with health education and proper slaughter practices, significantly reduces public health risks. 12. Pilot trials in Peru using oxfenbendazole (30 mg/kg) for pigs and praziquantel (5 mg/kg) for humans showed reductions in cysticercosis prevalence and incidence, though the parasite was not eliminated. A study in Cameroon using the TSOL18 vaccine and oxfenbendazole in pigs demonstrated the potential for eliminating the infection through combined approaches. 13. Rabies differs from most infections as clinical disease can be prevented through timely post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which includes wound treatment, rabies immune globulin, and vaccination. Widespread PEP has significantly reduced human rabies deaths, with over 10 million people receiving PEP annually, primarily in China and India. 14. PEP accounts for 80% of the estimated annual cost of rabies in Africa and Asia, with patient-borne costs comprising nearly half of the total. The frequency of PEP is expected to rise as safer cell-culture vaccines replace older nervous tissue-derived vaccines. 15. Snails act as vectors for trematode transmission, serving as obligatory intermediate hosts in their complex life cycles.
